explain.say: Hold an old Spanish silver coin from about 1600. Its silver was probably dug by Indigenous miners at Potosí in today's Bolivia, and it may have ended up in a merchant's chest in China. Global history follows journeys like this across borders. Look at the network: one metal linking three continents.

explain.say: Follow the links. From 1565 Spanish galleons sailed between Acapulco in Mexico and Manila in the Philippines, and Manila was founded as a Spanish city in 1571. Chinese merchants traded silk and porcelain there for American silver. China needed silver because its taxes were paid in it. Which way did the silk travel?

explain.say: Now see it on the map: the silver road from Bolivia across the Pacific to China, and another across the Atlantic to Spain. Historians Dennis Flynn and Arturo Giráldez argue global trade truly began in 1571, the year Manila linked the Americas to Asia. Would you call that the start of globalisation?

explain.say: Global historians use two tools. See the comparison. Kenneth Pomeranz's The Great Divergence, 2000, compared the Yangzi delta in China with England and asked why their paths split after 1800. Sanjay Subrahmanyam urged connected histories, following real links instead. Why does comparing help avoid treating Europe as the normal case?

explain.say: Global history pushes against Eurocentrism, meaning seeing the world as if Europe were its centre, though critics warn it can hide local detail. Great work. Your challenge: pick one object in your kitchen, tea, sugar or chilli, and trace how it first crossed an ocean.

faq.a: Global history studies the past across and beyond national borders, through connections like trade, migration and ideas, and through comparisons between regions. It grew strongly from the 1990s.

faq.q: Why did silver flow to China?
faq.a: Ming China collected more and more taxes in silver, especially after the Single Whip reforms, so silver was worth more there than elsewhere. Silver from Japan and the Americas flowed in, partly through Manila.

faq.a: The term, made famous by Kenneth Pomeranz in 2000, for the split after about 1800 when Western Europe pulled ahead economically. Pomeranz argued England and the Yangzi delta were similar until coal and colonies helped England.

Sanjay Subrahmanyam's term for histories that trace real links between societies, such as traders, empires and ideas moving between the Mughal, Ottoman and Iberian worlds, instead of treating each separately.

Eurocentrism means treating Europe's experience as the centre or the normal path of world history. Global historians try to correct it, for example in Dipesh Chakrabarty's Provincializing Europe, 2000.

facts: The Manila galleon trade between Acapulco and Manila ran from 1565 to 1815.
Manila was founded as a Spanish city in 1571.
